candidates.title: Graduated Autonomy for Artificial Intelligence Agents in Human Capital Management: A Systematic Review and a Consequence-Calibrated Governance Framework
candidates.abstract: Human capital management platforms are starting to embed software agents built on large language models. Unlike earlier analytics tools, these agents can plan a sequence of steps, call system functions and change employee records. Artificial intelligence is therefore moving from advising managers to acting for them. Most governance guidance, however, was written for systems that recommend rather than act. This study asks how organisations should match the autonomy of such agents to the consequences of the people decisions they touch. A systematic review was conducted and reported using the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Eighteen structured searches of a multi-source scholarly index returned 180 records. After duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 55 peer-reviewed sources were retained, and four foundational and regulatory sources were added. Thematic synthesis produced seven findings. Algorithmic control of work is already extensive. Bias in hiring tools is persistent and partly organisational. Human review is weaker than assumed, because reviewers often defer to machine advice. Responsibility tends to diffuse as systems gain autonomy. Employee trust depends on fair process and visible human involvement. Language-model agents add new failure modes, such as fabricated content and hidden instructions planted in documents. Finally, current governance frameworks rarely specify controls for individual delegated actions. Building on these findings, the study proposes a consequence-calibrated governance framework. It sets an autonomy ceiling for each class of people decision and links every ceiling to five control layers. Six testable propositions and practical guidance for human resource and technology leaders are offered. Keywords: large language models; people analytics; algorithmic management; automation bias; meaningful human control

candidates.title: Two-stage synthetic-to-real transfer learning for automated mammography report generation using vision-language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract We present a two-stage synthetic-to-real training pipeline for automated mammography report generation, together with a controlled, preregistered evaluation of whether its synthetic pretraining stage contributes to final report quality. Automated mammography report generation is constrained by the scarcity of paired mammogram-report data: public collections such as VinDr-Mammo and CBIS-DDSM provide structured annotations but no free-text reports. The pipeline converts BI-RADS annotations into synthetic reports (400 generated, 390 retained) to pretrain MedGemma-4B with multimodal LoRA, then fine-tunes on 407 real DMID reports. On the leak-free DMID test subset ( $$n = 49$$ ) it reaches ROUGE-L 0.656, METEOR 0.666, CIDEr 0.649 and BERTScore 0.917, exceeding every external baseline, including the published state of the art. The evaluation then shows that synthetic pretraining does not produce these numbers: the apparent advantage was measured between models of unequal adapter capacity, and at matched capacity the two schemes are equivalent. Across 60 training runs over three corpus sizes, three capacities and five initialisations, against a margin fixed in advance, no configuration favours two-stage training; capacity alone reproduces the gap. Two findings bear on evaluation. Under an assertion-level criterion no model fabricates findings on normal studies; the failure mode is omission. Textual and clinical quality diverge within one model: where two-stage training gains 0.058 ROUGE-L, BI-RADS agreement and sensitivity both fall. With agreement never exceeding $$\kappa = 0.14$$ , the obstacle to clinically useful reporting is diagnostic accuracy, not fluency.

candidates.title: PIX2DB: Reconstructing Executable Relational Databases from Document Images with a 2B Vision-Language Model
candidates.abstract: Abstract Tables trapped in screenshots, scans, receipts and charts are usually extracted as markup that keeps the layout but not the relational meaning: merged cells stay merged, an invoice header and its line items stay unrelated, and “$1,250.00” stays a string. We study image-to-database reconstruction: given one image, produce a SQLite dump whose schema, column types, keys and rows load and can be queried as they are. Training data with exact gold databases is obtained in two ways: by rendering samples of the Spider databases at six layout levels, and by converting PubTabNet, FinTabNet and CORD annotations under the same normalization rules. A 2B model (Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA) trained on 36,589 pairs and followed by a deterministic verify-and-repair layer reaches 0.86 table exact match and 0.99 foreign-key recall on rendered tables from unseen databases, against 0.75/0.75 for the 8B model of the same family prompted for SQL and 0.47/0.00 for an 8B HTML-to-SQLite pipeline. On held-out real images it obtains cell F1 0.81 (PubTabNet) and 0.96 (FinTabNet) and recall 0.93 on CORD receipt photos. On TabRecSet, a source not used in training, it is the best system that writes a database directly (0.52) but trails the 8B HTML pipeline (0.58), mostly in reading text from photographs. A variant trained on synthetic data alone matches the synthetic score and fails on real images, which locates the value of the real data. Code, model, data and all evaluation outputs are public.

candidates.title: Language and the measurement of social media engagement: a framework and research agenda
candidates.abstract: Purpose Ten years after Barger et al. (2016) reviewed consumer engagement on social media, this article revisits how engagement is measured. It reviews and integrates language-based measures of engagement, develops a conceptual framework and proposes a research agenda. Design/methodology/approach The article reviews the marketing and adjacent literature on measuring engagement from text, including natural language processing and large language model methods, organized by the cognitive, emotional and behavioral dimensions of engagement and across both the consumer and the firm. Findings Engagement counts capture the act of engagement but not its content. Language-based methods can in principle recover the cognitive and emotional dimensions that the consumer brand engagement construct names but that behavioral counts do not reach. The article maps the linguistic signals and measurement approaches available for each dimension on both sides of the consumer-firm dyad, separates what the literature supports from what remains to be done and identifies the conversation, rather than the isolated post, as the unit at which the co-creative process becomes measurable. Originality/value The article offers a framework that (1) distinguishes the engagement act from engagement content and positions language-based measurement as the means of recovering the latter, (2) extends to both parties of the consumer-firm dyad and locates the conversation as the unit of analysis, (3) states five testable propositions with boundary conditions and (4) sets out a prioritized agenda for research.
candidates.venue: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing

candidates.title: Effectiveness of structured cardiotocography training on practical performance and fetal trace interpretation among maternity nurses and midwives: a quasi-experimental controlled study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Cardiotocography (CTG) is widely used for intrapartum fetal monitoring, but the quality of monitoring depends in part on clinicians’ procedural performance and interpretation of fetal heart rate (FHR) traces. Structured competency-based education may strengthen these measured competencies. Aim To evaluate changes in practical CTG performance and FHR trace interpretation associated with a structured CTG training program among maternity nurses and midwives. Methods A non-randomized controlled quasi-experimental study included 64 maternity nurses and midwives at Al Thaghr General Hospital, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia (32 intervention; 32 control). Participants were allocated using a pre-specified non-random procedure based on duty rosters and clinical work schedules. The intervention comprised three standardized 45-60-minute sessions completed within the three-week intervention period. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, immediately after training, and at three-month follow-up using a 22-item CTG Performance Observational Checklist (0–22) and an 11-item FHR Trace Interpretation Assessment (0–11). Outcome assessors were independent of intervention delivery and blinded to group allocation. Mixed repeated-measures ANOVA tested group, time, and group x time effects; Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons examined change across time. Results All 64 participants completed all three assessments. Practical performance in the intervention group increased from 10.81 ± 2.16 at baseline to 18.31 ± 1.64 immediately post-training and 17.62 ± 1.70 at three months; the corresponding control-group means were 10.88 ± 2.11, 11.16 ± 2.20, and 10.97 ± 2.29. The group × time interaction was significant, F(2,124) = 712.17, p < .001, partial η² = 0.920. FHR interpretation showed a similar interaction, F(2,124) = 287.80, p < .001, partial η² = 0.823. In the intervention group, both outcomes declined modestly from immediate post-test to three months but remained significantly above baseline (Bonferroni-adjusted p < .001). Conclusion Structured CTG training was associated with substantial improvements in observed CTG performance and FHR trace interpretation, with scores remaining well above baseline at three months despite modest decline from the immediate post-test. The non-randomized allocation, single-center convenience sample, repeated use of the same assessment forms, and absence of maternal or neonatal outcome measures warrant cautious causal and clinical interpretation.

candidates.title: AgenticEvolve: Evolutionary Program Search with Persistent Language Model Agents that Design and Run Experiments
candidates.abstract: Evolutionary program search with large language models keeps the structure of an evolutionary algorithm and uses the model as its variation operator. Typically, the model generates each candidate program in a single request from parent programs and their scores. We present AgenticEvolve, an evolutionary program search framework in which each island is run by a persistent large language model agent. Between evaluations, the agent designs and runs experiments on the candidate program. To measure the contribution of experimentation, we compare AgenticEvolve with No-analysis, an otherwise identical configuration with experiments disabled. On two heuristic design tasks with three large language models, AgenticEvolve produces better programs than No-analysis and OpenEvolve on both hidden and unseen instances. It reaches the baselines' final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground-truth structure of more equations than No-analysis and existing language-model and genetic programming baselines.

candidates.title: AI-Based PDF Chat and Summarization Engine Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Prof. Dr. Aniruddha Rumale, Dr. Sushma Zade
candidates.abstract: Portable Document Format (PDF) files are the most common way of storing reports, research papers, manuals, and legal documents, but their layout-oriented structure makes them difficult to search and to query conversationally. Large Language Models (LLMs) can answer questions fluently, but they may hallucinate and cannot process long documents that exceed a fixed context window. This study presents the design, implementation, and preliminary testing of a PDF chat and summarization system based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system uses a three-stage data pipeline (raw, processed, and RAG-ready) that parses PDFs, removes repeating headers and footers, converts content to Markdown, and applies structure-aware chunking, which attaches section-path metadata to every chunk. Answers are generated by the openai/gpt-oss-120b model (served through the Groq API) using passages retrieved from a local ChromaDB vector store with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings, and are returned with page references. Three chunking strategies (fixed-size, Markdown-aware, and hierarchical) are defined, and an evaluation protocol based on answer accuracy, faithfulness, hit rate at k, unsupported-answer rate, and response time is specified for comparing them. In preliminary testing, the system processed uploaded PDFs and answered natural-language questions with an average response time of approximately 2–5 seconds. A full comparative evaluation is left for future work. The study provides a reproducible, small-scale baseline that student and small-team developers can extend, and it argues that document preprocessing and chunking quality are central to the reliability of PDF question answering
candidates.venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

candidates.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
candidates.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.

candidates.title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
candidates.abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

candidates.title: Federated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.

candidates.title: Evidence-Grounded Retrieval- Augmented Generation and Knowledge-Graph Grounding for Patient-Safety Reasoning: A Comparative Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models offer promising capabilities for clinical reasoning, but unsupported claims, hallucinations, limited evidence traceability, and inconsistent reasoning constrain their use in patient-safety applications. Retrieval-augmented generation and structured knowledge representations may complement each other to improve output reliability. Objective This study evaluated whether grounding a LLaMA-based large language model in retrieved evidence, structured patient-safety knowledge, or both improves the factual correctness, evidence grounding, safety, explainability, and clinical usefulness of patient-safety reasoning while reducing hallucinations and unsupported claims. Methods We conducted a controlled comparative evaluation using patient-safety cases derived from critical care data and aligned with established patient-safety and clinical terminology frameworks. The same underlying language model, case inputs, prompting strategy, and output format were evaluated under four conditions: LLM only, LLM with retrieval-augmented generation, LLM with knowledge-graph and ontology grounding, and LLM with combined retrieval and knowledge-graph/ontology grounding. Model outputs were evaluated across six predefined dimensions: factual correctness, evidence grounding, hallucination or unsupported claims, safety, explainability, and clinical usefulness. Pairwise comparisons, confidence intervals, effect sizes, and appropriate statistical tests were used to assess differences between conditions. Expert assessment was also used to examine the relevance and interpretability of generated outputs. Results Grounding substantially improved patient-safety reasoning compared with the ungrounded model. The combined condition demonstrated the strongest overall performance across factual correctness, evidence grounding, safety, explainability, and clinical usefulness, while producing the lowest level of hallucination and unsupported claims. Retrieval primarily strengthened the use and traceability of external evidence, whereas knowledge-graph and ontology grounding provided structured semantic context for linking clinical concepts, medications, conditions, procedures, and safety events. Combining the two mechanisms produced more consistent and comprehensive reasoning than either grounding approach alone. Expert assessment further indicated that grounded outputs were more interpretable and useful for safety-oriented review. Conclusions Evidence retrieval and structured knowledge representation provide complementary forms of grounding for large language models used in patient-safety reasoning. Their combination can improve the reliability, transparency, and practical usefulness of model-generated safety assessments. The findings support further prospective evaluation of grounded language models within clinical workflows, with particular attention to claim-level verification, human oversight, workflow integration, and safety assurance.

candidates.title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
candidates.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.

candidates.title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.

candidates.title: When News Gets Old: Portfolio Allocation with Reinforcement Learning and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Financial news can influence investment decisions long after publication. Timely news may reach an investor before prices fully adjust, whereas older news may already be reflected in prices. We examine two ways to handle aging signals: retain them and give a portfolio policy timing information, or filter them out before portfolio selection. A fixed large language model (LLM) extracts signals from public SEC disclosures. We compare these treatments in reinforcement learning (RL) policies and LLMs that choose portfolios directly. We evaluate returns after trading costs in historical tests over 2023-2025. RL choices respond to timing information in a controlled test, but historical returns show no consistent benefit from adding it. For the LLM, filtering old news produced the highest average net return, reaching 18.43% per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks. This exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.

candidates.title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
candidates.abstract: Large language models trained on data generated by other models can sometimes inherit traits unrelated to that data, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. We study both hard label distillation, where students train on numbers generated by a biased teacher, and on-policy soft label distillation, where students generate the data and the teacher's logits provide the learning signal. Using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo models, we find that transfer persists in both settings across differences in weight initialization, pretraining data order, pretraining corpus, model size, and architecture. Across pretraining checkpoints, the ability to transmit a preference and the ability to acquire one develop separately: some checkpoints are more effective teachers but weaker students, and vice versa. Consistent with this distinction, cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric in magnitude when teacher and student roles are reversed. To investigate what carries the preference signal, we construct synthetic number sequences that match the teacher's generated number frequencies but have no dependence on the prompt or preceding numbers and find that these still induce substantial transfer in the hard-label setting. In top-$K$ soft-label distillation, removing animal tokens from the loss reduces transfer, although not completely in the same-model setting. In our experiments, soft label distillation produces more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard label distillation. The growing use of on-policy distillation in model post-training makes this a particularly relevant setting for assessing unintended preference transfer.

candidates.title: The Geometry of Metaphor: Probing and Steering Metaphor Representations in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Metaphor is a crucial aspect of human cognition. As such, we would like to understand how it is represented in large language models (LLMs) and how it might be controlled. We use mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify causal subspaces in a range of LLMs covering different architectures and sizes. We show that we are able to steer output on classification tasks across different parts of speech. We are also able to steer output on generation tasks, indicating that these techniques can be used to control the metaphoricity of LLM output.

candidates.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.

candidates.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

candidates.title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

candidates.title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
candidates.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross-layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine-tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight-only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune-or-Prioritize Mixed-Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width assignment. It allows higher-precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit-budget utilization. Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.

candidates.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

candidates.title: Performance of latest-generation large language models on endodontic specialty examination questions: a comparative cross-sectional study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background This study aimed to compare the performance of Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, ChatGPT 5.2, and DeepSeek V3.2 on the Endodontics section of the Turkish Dental Specialty Exam (DUS), with particular attention to question source, type, and endodontic subtopic. Methods The dataset comprised 187 endodontic questions from 2012–2025, stratified into internet-sourced from 2012–2021 ( n = 127) and textbook-sourced from 2022–2025 ( n = 60). Questions were further categorized by type as case analysis, literature knowledge, combination or visual analysis, and by 10 endodontic subtopics. Following a standardized zero-shot prompting protocol (public web interfaces, default settings, single run per item), two independent endodontic assessors scored responses on a blinded 0–3 rubric, and then the two evaluator scores were averaged for each response. Overall model performance was expressed as a percentage of the maximum possible rubric score (100%). Statistical analysis employed the Friedman test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests with Bonferroni correction, Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests. Results All reported percentages represent normalized rubric-based performance scores, evaluating both answer selection and reasoning quality, rather than simple correct/incorrect accuracy rates. High inter-rater agreement was achieved, with quadratic weighted kappa values ranging from 0.954 to 0.998. In overall performance, Gemini 3 Pro (90.37%) and Gemini 3 Flash (88.32%) significantly outperformed ChatGPT 5.2 (78.25%) and DeepSeek V3.2 (62.12%) (adjusted p ≤ 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.214); corresponding answer accuracies were 94.1%, 93.0%, 86.6%, and 73.3%. No significant difference was found between the Gemini models (adjusted p = 1.000). No significant difference was observed between internet-sourced and textbook-sourced questions within any model. In literature knowledge questions, combination questions, and selected endodontic subtopics, the Gemini models generally showed higher rubric-based performance than the other models. Conclusions The findings indicate high rubric-based performance of the latest-generation LLMs, particularly the Gemini 3 series, on Turkish endodontics residency examination questions. No significant difference in performance was observed between internet-sourced and textbook-sourced questions; however, contamination of the data in both groups cannot be excluded. These models may serve as adjunctive tools in endodontic education; however, examination performance does not establish clinical diagnostic performance, and their outputs require expert validation.

candidates.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language
candidates.abstract: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p<0.001). (2) YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B significantly outperforms Mistral-7B and Phi-3-mini on multiclass classification, BPB and native-speaker ratings (mean 3.28 vs 2.52 and 2.22; n=100; alpha=0.69-0.77; p<0.05); on binary classification its QLoRA advantage is not significant (p>=0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. candidates.title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their use as the backbone of foundation recommendation models (FRMs). Existing methods enhance recommendations through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning under a Think-then-Answer paradigm. However, explicit CoT incurs substantial inference overhead by generating lengthy reasoning traces and relies on manually designed templates that struggle to capture diverse, dynamic user interests. We propose OneLatent, an efficient latent reasoning framework that compresses explicit reasoning traces into several learnable latent tokens, enabling Latent-Reason-then-Answer inference without generating verbose traces. OneLatent first introduces Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT), which creates diverse, high-quality teacher-generated supervision by exploring user interests from multiple perspectives and automatically adapting reasoning complexity to each instance. Building on pretrained FRMs, it then uses a three-stage latent-token alignment paradigm to progressively internalize CoT traces into learnable latent tokens. Finally, a multistage curriculum-based post-training strategy activates latent-token reasoning for downstream recommendation tasks. Experiments on an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark show that OneLatent consistently outperforms explicit CoT-based methods and traditional baselines. Compared with the Think and No-Think variants of FRMs, OneLatent improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, while achieving over 17x higher online inference throughput. We further develop a production serving system for scalable, real-time FRM inference. An online A/B test in Kuaishou's local-services advertising scenario shows that deploying OneLatent with this system yields an estimated 9.6% revenue lift over strong online baselines, including OneRec and OneReason.

candidates.title: Meaning Contracts: Local Semantic Geometry in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.

candidates.title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
candidates.abstract: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.

candidates.title: How Ground Truth Shapes Retrieval Scores: Evidence-Aware Evaluation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Breast Lesions
candidates.abstract: Purpose: To describe an evidence-aware retrieval evaluation protocol for a clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over breast lesion management literature, addressing the dependence of retrieval scores on annotation coverage. Methods: An 18-document corpus and an 18-query development benchmark, with one Yes/No or WH-question per document, were used. Retrieval combined dense embeddings, BM25, and cross-encoder reranking. Chunk sizes of 128 to 1024 tokens, overlaps of 0 to 20%, and four retriever configurations were evaluated. Relevance was defined by evidence spans mapped to all containing chunks, treating overlapping chunks with equivalent evidence as relevant. Retrieval was evaluated using R-Precision, Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG@K. Separately, generation was assessed on a 512-token index at K=1 to 5 using DeepEval claim-level metrics, with deepseek-v4-pro as the LLM judge, and BLEU/ROUGE metrics. Results: The selected hybrid retriever, using 384-token chunks and 20% overlap, retrieved accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries. Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3 each reached 0.94. Ground-truth curation increased evidence spans from 25 to 37 and accepted chunk targets from 36 to 51 without changing retrieval rankings. Conclusion: Cross-encoder reranking achieved the highest retrieval scores. Expanded relevance annotations increased recognized evidence without changing rankings, highlighting annotation sensitivity. The small development set and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist assessment of evidence sufficiency.

candidates.title: Harnessing Language Models as Optimization Modeling Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver programs, but reliably producing correct formulations and implementations remains challenging. Existing approaches improve optimization modeling through agentic workflows or task-specific post-training. This raises a practical question: can a lightweight harness using a single model role achieve competitive performance without additional training? We introduce OPTICYCLE and OPTISTATE, two lightweight inference harnesses for optimization modeling, and evaluate them on nine benchmarks comprising 2,634 problems using 11 Qwen variants spanning 0.6B-27B parameters. Our results show that execution-guided revision consistently improves macro accuracy over direct generation for all evaluated models, with gains of up to 49.46 percentage points. Despite their simplicity, both harnesses outperform six adapted agentic workflows in same-model comparisons and four evaluated post-trained optimization models at comparable model sizes, without additional training. Explicit formulation state provides further but model-dependent improvements, suggesting that additional structure is not universally beneficial.

candidates.title: Evaluating Retrieval Accuracy and Latency for Enterprise RAG Systems on FiQA
candidates.abstract: Abstract Retrieval design influences which evidence a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system can access and how long that evidence takes to obtain. This study compares TF-IDF, BM25, a dynamically quantized MiniLM dense retriever, and reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) of BM25 and MiniLM on the complete BEIR FiQA test split. All 648 test questions were evaluated against 57,638 documents using the supplied relevance judgments. Outcomes were nDCG@10, the proportion of questions with a relevant document in the first five results (Hit@5), recall, reciprocal rank, and local CPU retrieval latency. Accuracy uncertainty was estimated with 10,000 paired query bootstrap samples; latency was measured over three randomized passes. Mean nDCG@10 was 0.179 for TF-IDF, 0.235 for BM25, 0.334 for MiniLM, and 0.337 for RRF. RRF minus MiniLM was +0.003 (95% confidence interval -0.015 to +0.022). Hit@5 ranged from 30.2% to 54.0%; median retrieval latency ranged from 5.74 to 23.92 ms. The results quantify implementation-specific effectiveness and latency trade-offs and show why fusion should be evaluated against its strongest constituent. FiQA is a public financial forum benchmark, and the evaluated model may have encountered overlapping training material. These findings concern retrieval relevance under the supplied judgments, not generated-answer accuracy or production enterprise performance.

candidates.title: Dialect-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Arabic Question Answering: Measuring and Mitigating the Moroccan Darija–MSA Retrieval Gap
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for Arabic are evaluated almost exclusively with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) queries, although users write in dialect. We study this mismatch with a parallel benchmark of 200 questions written in both MSA and Moroccan Darija over 3,054 Arabic Wikipedia passages. Dialectal queries lower hybrid-retrieval Recall@1 from 0.755 to 0.620, and the loss reaches the answers: with five retrieved passages, answer correctness falls from 0.810 to 0.690, mostly through additional refusals; part of this loss persists even when the gold passage is supplied directly, so retrieval is the larger but not the only component. Rewriting Darija queries into MSA does not help. Zero-shot cross-encoder reranking raises dialectal Recall@1 to 0.800 (MSA: 0.755 unreranked, 0.875 reranked) and lets a single retrieved passage replace five unreranked passages with no loss larger than five percentage points and a 3.7-fold shorter prompt. Because dialectal queries are retrieved with lower confidence, gating the reranker on the retriever’s score margin concentrates its cost on them without any dialect detection, retaining 94% of the benefit while reranking about half of the queries. The findings hold under a human-validated LLM judge (Cohen’s κ=0.797), Holm correction and three prompt wordings, and replicate judge-free on a second, Darija-trained generator. We release the benchmark, corpus, code and all result files.

candidates.title: Constraint Reasoning and Large Language Models Join Forces: Providing Contrastive Explanations for Real-World Optimisation-Based Applications
candidates.abstract: We focus on optimisation-based Decision Support Systems in real-world applications. In this context, we aim to provide contrastive explanations that answer users' questions about recommendations based on the solution of an optimisation problem, specifically a Mixed-Integer Program (MIP). Addressing this endeavour is crucial to ensure human oversight of the decisions implemented, as required by international guidelines on trustworthy and responsible automated decision-making systems. We propose a novel methodology that combines constraint reasoning techniques and Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate contrastive explanations for optimisation problems encoded as MIPs. Although LLMs have shown impressive capabilities in Natural Language processing, they can produce incorrect answers due to reasoning limitations. To overcome these limitations, we leverage constraint reasoning techniques to distil the information necessary to produce an explanation, which is then passed as input to an LLM as the so-called graph of reasons. Such a graph captures the semantics and the relationships among constraints of the optimisation problem. Results on real-world scheduling domains show that incorporating constraint reasoning improves explanations generated by the LLM. In particular, using the graph of reasons enables the LLM to produce natural-language explanations that include more relevant reasons while reducing errors compared to explanations generated without this structure.

candidates.title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks
candidates.abstract: Knowledge graph-to-text (KG-to-text) generation verbalizes a set of knowledge graph triples into fluent natural language. While fine-tuned encoder-decoder models have long been the standard approach, recent LLMs are becoming increasingly competitive. We benchmark recent LLMs against fine-tuned encoder-decoder models, using reference-based metrics and graph-grounded reference-free LLM-based evaluation validated against human annotations. We observed that recent LLMs substantially narrow, and in several settings close, the gap with fine-tuned models on reference-based metrics, while performing better on graph-grounded metrics. LLM-based evaluation scores show limited correlation with reference-based metrics, suggesting that the two approaches capture different aspects of generation quality. Graph-grounded evaluation reveals that prompted models produce fewer contradictions and triple omissions than fine-tuned models, and these errors increase more rapidly with graph size for fine-tuned models, highlighting differences between the two approaches that reference-based metrics may not fully capture.

candidates.title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
candidates.abstract: Reusable skills allow large language model agents to package task-specific procedures, tool affordances, and execution guidance into modular units. Prior work has largely studied how agents retrieve, compose, or synthesize skills before execution. In coding agents, however, execution poses an additional runtime control problem: the same task may be solved through primitive tool calls, macro skills, or hybrid execution that starts with a macro and falls back to micro-level recovery. We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures. The system combines a feature-based granularity controller and a finite-state recovery executor. We evaluate the framework with a deterministic coding-agent protocol using verifier-defined success, total cost, and process metrics such as macro adoption, failure recovery, route match, and transition correctness. Results show that fixed macro execution is efficient when applicable but brittle under mismatch, while runtime routing and explicit macro-to-micro recovery improve robustness and recover controlled macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved. Our findings suggest that skill libraries for coding agents should be treated not only as retrievable resources, but also as controllable, verifiable, and recoverable execution abstractions.

candidates.title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models
candidates.abstract: Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy-preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision-oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev-Data, a source-grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical-decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline-grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B-9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4-23.0 points. RetiJev-9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4-6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.

candidates.title: ReflectPO: Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: With external tools, large language models (LLMs) can tackle complex tasks through sustained environmental interaction. LLM-based agents are therefore increasingly used to tackle complex long-horizon tasks in real-world environments. However, these tasks involve sequential, interdependent decisions and changes in environmental states. Early execution errors affect subsequent interaction histories and environmental states, and their effects accumulate along the decision chain. To address this challenge, we propose Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization (ReflectPO), a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous error recovery in long-horizon tasks. ReflectPO comprises two core components. The first is Reflection-Guided Sampling. We use branch differences and repeated visits in interaction trajectories to construct hints for error recovery. The second is Tree-Structured Credit Assignment. We organize sampled trajectories into trees and assign action-level credit using parent--child reward differences and recovery gains. Experiments over two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks show that ReflectPO outperforms multiple existing baselines in most domains. It also achieves the best overall performance on average. Further analyses show that ReflectPO effectively improves agents' ability to recognize their own deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue making progress toward task completion.

candidates.title: IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities for Agentic CLI Systems
candidates.abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

candidates.title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference
candidates.abstract: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.

candidates.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
candidates.abstract: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Taxpayer Advisory in an LMIC Setting: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of Statutory Legal Retrieval

This study developed and evaluated a proof-of-concept retrieval-augmented generation framework for taxpayer advisory using national income-tax legislation as an authoritative knowledge source. The objective was to test whether semantic retrieval could identify statutory provisions accurately enough to support grounded downstream language-model prompting. The legislation was transformed into 198 knowledge units, embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, indexed in ChromaDB, and evaluated using 900 automatically generated questions linked to expected provisions. Results The retriever achieved 72.00% Top-1 accuracy, 86.78% Top-3 accuracy, 28.93% Precision@3, 86.78% Recall@3, and mean reciprocal rank 0.7880. Many Top-1 errors were recovered within the first three results, indicating ranking ambiguity among semantically related provisions rather than complete retrieval failure. The prototype integrated legal document processing, vector search, provision retrieval and structured prompt construction in an end-to-end workflow. The results support technical feasibility for grounded taxpayer information, but generation quality, legal correctness, usability and compliance effects were not evaluated. Validation should include additional tax instruments, real taxpayer queries, professional legal review, multilingual support and cross-jurisdiction testing before deployment in resource-constrained public-service settings.

candidates.title: RAG-Assert: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Assertion Generation for Automated Unit Testing
candidates.abstract: Test assertions are a key mechanism for validating program behavior in unit testing, and their quality determines the defect detection capability and engineering utility of automated tests. Existing assertion generation approaches fall into two main categories: deep learning-based methods, which are sensitive to training data scale and suffer from limited generalization, and retrieval-based methods, which rely on shallow lexical similarity and fail to capture deep code semantics. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Retrieval-Augmented Assertion Generation (RAG-Assert), a retrieval-augmented assertion generation method for automated unit testing. RAG-Assert constructs a hybrid retriever that combines token-level Jaccard similarity and CFG-derived basic-block semantic similarity to retrieve the most relevant historical assertion from the retrieval repository for a given focal test. The retrieved assertion is incorporated as external knowledge context during fine-tuning and generation of a pretrained code model. A beam-search decoding strategy is further adopted to select the reliable assertion from multiple candidates, reducing the probability of generating semantically inconsistent assertions. Experiments on the Methods2Test dataset demonstrate that RAG-Assert consistently outperforms five representative baseline methods across multiple metrics including Top-1 accuracy, Top-10 accuracy, and Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score. Evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark further confirms the practical defect detection capability of the proposed method. Ablation studies validate the complementary advantages of combining token-level similarity and CFG-derived basic-block semantic similarity in the hybrid retriever.

candidates.title: Automated Enrichment Analysis with GraphRAG: Efficient Multi-Database ORA Extraction and Biological Interpretation
candidates.abstract: Over-representation analysis (ORA) is widely used to interpret gene-expression studies, but its outputs are often fragmented across gene-set databases and presented as flat term lists that obscure gene-level links among related enrichment signals. We propose Graph-Based Over-Representation Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GBOR-RAG), an integrated and traceable framework for ORA interpretation. GBOR-RAG represents heterogeneous gene-set databases as a unified term--gene knowledge graph, where shared genes connect related terms across sources. After graph-based ORA scoring, the framework retrieves a compact connected evidence subgraph that preserves both cross-database relationships and gene-level support. The subgraph conditions an LLM to generate biological interpretations, and we introduce a claim-level faithfulness metric to assess whether generated claims are supported by explicit evidence. Experiments show that graph-based ORA preserves conventional ORA results with high consistency (mean Pearson $r=0.997$) while reducing query time by a median of $37\times$ (up to $48\times$). The retrieved subgraphs average 36.8 nodes and achieve the highest overall integration score (4.12), and GBOR-RAG attains the highest claim-level faithfulness (0.90) among the compared systems. Adding a PubMed literature layer further improves the overall interpretation quality from 4.17 to 4.75.

candidates.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
candidates.abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

candidates.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
candidates.abstract: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. candidates.title: Verbalizing Activation Differences with Natural Language Autoencoders
candidates.abstract: Activation verbalizers translate the internal representations of large language models into human-readable text. The recently proposed natural language autoencoders (NLAs) learn this by reconstructing activations through a natural language bottleneck. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond the setting they were trained for. Here, we study this question for NLAs along four closely related questions: (i) Do NLA verbalizations exhibit compositional structure with respect to their input? (ii) Do NLAs generalize to finetuned versions of the model they were trained for? (iii) Can NLAs recover finetuning objectives in model diffing? (iv) Can NLAs be specialized for model diffing? Across four models from three families, our experiments provide evidence supporting a largely positive answer to all four questions. Specifically, verbalizations of composed analogy activations mostly name the target while rarely mentioning the subtracted word, and an NLA can be reused on lightweight finetunes of its original model without retraining, with reconstruction quality degrading noticeably only for the largest model. Verbalizing activation differences between Taboo model organisms and their original models recovers the concealed secret word for most organisms, and reinforcement learning on activation differences further improves this recovery on held-out organisms. We also find that NLAs can recover the finetuning objective without the finetuned model generating any token, since the most informative token positions precede the user prompt. NLAs do not yet match state-of-the-art model diffing methods on the emergent misalignment detection task, but outperform a blackbox baseline. Our findings suggest that NLAs can meaningfully verbalize differences in activation space, rendering NLAs a promising direction for future work.

candidates.title: ValuSpec: Plug-and-Play Candidate Valuation before Target Verification for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
candidates.abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel. However, in practical serving scenarios, similar requests repeatedly induce overlapping candidate branches. While retrieval-based methods mitigate this by reusing historical drafts, the resulting candidate trees often contain many low-quality branches as the candidate tree grows, which reduces verification efficiency and wastes target-side computation. To address this, we propose ValuSpec, a plug-and-play candidate valuation mechanism that filters low-quality branches from a supplied candidate tree before expensive target-side verification. ValuSpec introduces transfer-based supervision to align filtering with the target model's behavior. A filtering threshold is estimated from the target model's greedy trajectories on a calibration split, without any parameter training. The target model then verifies the filtered tree under the output-identical greedy rule, so accepted tokens are guaranteed to match standard autoregressive decoding exactly. Experimental results on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench show that, in our main evaluation, ValuSpec achieves up to 2.38x end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based tree settings. Furthermore, integrating ValuSpec into the EAGLE-3 dynamic tree framework yields up to 2.78x end-to-end speedup without modifying its tree construction strategy, demonstrating that ValuSpec serves as a generally applicable and plug-and-play candidate valuation module.

candidates.title: VERA: A Responsible AI Dashboard for Assessing LLM Deployments in Light of the EU AI Act
candidates.abstract: Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.

candidates.title: Tracing Hallucinations in LLM Reasoning for UML Class Diagram Generation: An Empirical Taxonomy and Mitigation Study
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate UML class diagrams from natural language requirements, but hallucinations may compromise the correctness and completeness of the resulting diagrams. Existing evaluations mostly assess the final diagram, without examining the intermediate traces of reasoning-capable LLMs, which can reveal where these hallucinations arise. We develop an empirical taxonomy of eleven hallucination sub-types organised into three dimensions: Prompt Faithfulness (deviations between requirements and reasoning), Code Faithfulness (discrepancies between reasoning and generated PlantUML code), and Reasoning Quality (problems within the reasoning). The taxonomy was derived from 60 manually annotated DeepSeek-R1 traces, applied to 120 further DeepSeek-R1 traces through a dual-LLM annotation pipeline, and examined on 20 DeepSeek-V4-Pro traces. Code Faithfulness was the most frequent dimension for DeepSeek-R1 in both datasets, whereas Prompt Faithfulness dominated for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, suggesting model-dependent failure patterns. In the manually annotated traces, reasoning-trace length showed no significant monotonic association with hallucination frequency, whereas requirement complexity was negatively associated with it, particularly for Prompt Faithfulness errors. In a mitigation experiment on 13 Golden UML ModelSet cases with three Qwen3-based models, adding Prompt Faithfulness and Reasoning Quality constraints to the generation prompt raised the pooled mean F1 score by 4.0 percentage points, whereas a post-hoc Code Faithfulness review provided no consistent further benefit. Relationship modelling remained the lowest-scoring element throughout. These results suggest that localising hallucinations within the generation process can inform targeted, prompt-based mitigation. Whether these findings generalise beyond the DeepSeek and Qwen3 model families remains to be tested.
